title: Service Business Capacity Planning Template With Example
intro: A service business capacity plan compares committed work with the hours and skills actually available to deliver it. Use this worksheet before accepting another project or hiring another employee.
fields: Separate specialist work from general support; hours are not interchangeable.
Start with scheduled hours for each person.
Deduct leave, training, internal meetings, and management responsibilities.
Paid hours minus unavailable hours; reserve a deliberate allowance for interruptions.
Estimate remaining hours on signed projects by role and delivery week.
Available delivery hours minus committed demand; a negative result needs a decision.
steps: List the next four weeks of signed delivery commitments. Ask the people doing the work to estimate remaining effort, rather than using the original quote unchanged.
Compare demand and available hours for each skill. A surplus in administration cannot resolve a shortage of licensed technical capacity.
Move discretionary work, renegotiate a milestone, or use qualified outside support before promising new dates. Record who can approve each option.
example: Illustrative example: three consultants have 120 paid hours in a week. Leave and internal work consume 30 hours, leaving 90 delivery hours. Signed projects require 105 hours. The 15-hour deficit remains even if total company headcount looks adequate. Moving a 20-hour workshop into the following week creates five hours of headroom, provided the client agrees.
failure: Planning everyone at 100% delivery utilization leaves no room for corrections or urgent customer needs. Set a buffer from your actual interruption history and revisit it after the first month.
measure: Track estimated versus actual delivery hours, overdue milestones, and overtime by role. Review weekly; investigate a growing backlog before treating higher utilization as success.

title: Sales to Operations Handoff Checklist for Service Firms
intro: A sales to operations handoff checklist transfers the commitments behind a sale to the team responsible for delivery. The receiving owner must accept the brief before a kickoff date becomes a customer promise.
fields: Link the accepted agreement and list exclusions.
Record what the buyer expects to be different after delivery.
Include unusual deadlines, integrations, and dependencies.
Record payment prerequisites and approved billing terms.
Name the person accepting responsibility and their backup.
Accepted, returned for clarification, or conditionally accepted with named blockers.
steps: Ask sales to complete the brief using the signed agreement and discovery notes. Label assumptions explicitly instead of presenting them as accepted scope.
Have delivery check effort, staffing, access, and deadlines. Return incomplete briefs with a specific missing item and a responsible person.
Introduce the customer to the delivery owner with the next action and confirmed date. Keep unresolved sales promises visible through the first milestone.
example: Illustrative example: a seller promises a CRM migration before month-end, but delivery discovers that the customer has not provided an export. The handoff records data access as a blocking dependency. Delivery offers a revised date tied to receipt of a usable export, and sales confirms that change with the buyer before kickoff.
failure: Changing a CRM stage to closed-won is not evidence that delivery accepted the job. Separate commercial close from operational acceptance so sold work does not silently enter an unstaffed queue.
measure: Measure time from signature to accepted handoff, returned briefs, and first-milestone delays caused by missing sales information.

title: Decision Rights Matrix Template for Small Business Teams
intro: A decision rights matrix explains who may make a recurring decision, what limits apply, and when escalation is required. It is useful when routine approvals keep returning to the owner despite clear job titles.
fields: Describe a specific choice, such as approving a refund.
Assign one role with final authority within the boundary.
Identify people whose information is necessary.
State financial, customer, quality, or timing limits.
Describe the condition requiring a higher decision.
Identify where the reasoning and outcome are saved.
steps: Review the owner's last ten interruptions and group repeated approval requests. Start with frequent, reversible decisions.
Agree on boundaries with the responsible manager. Discuss both a normal case and an exception so the limit is understandable.
Run a two-week pilot. Review decisions after they happen within the agreed boundary, and change unclear rules instead of taking every decision back.
example: Illustrative example: an account manager may approve a service credit up to $250 for a documented delivery error. A credit above that amount or a complaint involving a contractual dispute goes to the general manager. The account manager logs the reason and notifies finance so the credit appears correctly on the invoice.
failure: Assigning accountability without access to information or spending authority creates another approval queue. Give the role the tools needed to act and name a backup for absences.
measure: Track owner approvals per week, time waiting for a decision, and decisions later reversed because a boundary was unclear.

title: Change Order Process Template for Service Businesses
intro: A change order process makes new requests visible before they consume delivery capacity. Use it when extra revisions, added locations, or new deliverables turn a profitable project into unpriced work.
fields: Describe the requested difference from the agreed scope.
Estimate added work and any external purchases.
Name the internal approver and customer acceptance evidence.
Record the revised plan, invoice action, and team notification.
steps: Capture the request in plain language and compare it with the signed scope. Resolve genuine ambiguity before assuming the customer owes an additional fee.
Estimate the full impact, including review time and dependencies. Offer a tradeoff such as replacing a planned deliverable where that is practical.
Obtain the required acceptance before starting changed work. Update the project plan and billing record together so operations and finance use the same version.
example: Illustrative example: a client requests a second training session for another department. The original package includes one session. The manager proposes an additional session with preparation time and a revised completion date. The team schedules it after acceptance, rather than absorbing the work and disputing the invoice later.
failure: Calling every small clarification a change order creates friction. Define what is included, what counts as a correction, and what requires a commercial decision at kickoff.
measure: Compare approved extra effort with unbilled extra hours, approval turnaround, and milestone changes. Review repeated requests when updating future scopes.

title: Client Onboarding Workflow for Missing Documents
intro: An onboarding workflow for missing documents separates a stalled customer dependency from an internal delivery failure. It gives every missing item an owner, a due date, and a consequence for the project schedule.
fields: Name the specific document, period, and acceptable format.
Explain which delivery step depends on it.
Name the person expected to provide it.
Tie the request to an agreed milestone.
Record whether the received item is complete and usable.
Name the contact and schedule action if the deadline passes.
steps: Build the request list from actual delivery requirements. Remove items that are merely convenient so the customer can see what really blocks progress.
Send a consolidated request with a secure collection method appropriate to the information. Confirm receipt and validate usability before marking an item complete.
Use a scheduled exception review to escalate overdue dependencies. Explain any proposed milestone change to the customer and document the agreed next step.
example: Illustrative example: a project requires twelve monthly reports but receives only the latest quarter. The coordinator records nine missing periods, explains which analysis cannot begin, and gives one consolidated request to the customer contact. Partial receipt does not trigger a misleading completed status.
failure: Sending automated reminders indefinitely can conceal a relationship problem. After a defined number of attempts, ask a person to resolve ownership, access, or a misunderstood request.
measure: Monitor days waiting for customer inputs, requests returned as unusable, and kickoff-to-ready time. Keep customer waiting time separate from internal processing time.

title: CRM Data Cleanup Checklist Before Sales Automation
intro: A CRM data cleanup checklist prepares contact and opportunity records for reliable follow-up. Clean the rules behind the records before turning on automation that can multiply mistakes.
fields: Every active opportunity needs one accountable seller.
Choose matching rules and inspect ambiguous matches manually.
Define what must be true for each opportunity stage.
Record a specific action, due date, and owner.
Preserve communication preferences and suppression records.
Close or archive stale opportunities with a recorded reason.
steps: Export a recoverable backup and test cleanup on a small sample. Preserve notes, activities, associations, and permission history when evaluating merges.
Agree on field definitions and a source of truth for conflicting values. Review high-value opportunities manually before changing ownership or stage.
Run reports for missing owners, overdue actions, and impossible stage sequences. Enable automation only after a seller can explain and trust the cleaned sample.
example: Illustrative example: two records for the same buyer have different email preferences. A blind merge could reactivate outreach to someone who opted out. The cleanup preserves the restrictive preference, checks associated opportunities, and records which record survived before any follow-up sequence runs.
failure: Deleting old records to improve dashboard appearance can erase useful loss history. Use lifecycle statuses and retention rules appropriate to your business instead of treating age alone as a deletion instruction.
measure: Track duplicate creation, active deals without next actions, and automation exceptions. Review the intake process if the same problems return each week.

title: Lead Response Time SLA Template for Small Sales Teams
intro: A lead response service standard defines when a new inquiry receives a useful human response and who covers the queue. Set a realistic promise based on staffing and business hours rather than an arbitrary speed target.
fields: Separate quote requests, referrals, general questions, and existing-client issues.
Specify days, time zone, holidays, and after-hours handling.
Define the elapsed or staffed time allowed.
Name the primary responder and backup.
Define what counts beyond an automated receipt.
Assign escalation when the response target is missed.
steps: Measure a week of inquiry arrival times and current response delays. Include forms, calls, email, and referral messages so hidden queues are visible.
Assign coverage by shift or queue. Route existing-customer issues appropriately rather than mixing urgent delivery problems with new sales inquiries.
Test an inquiry during coverage and outside it. Verify assignment, notification, backup access, and reporting before promising the standard publicly.
example: Illustrative example: a two-person sales team commits to a useful response within two staffed hours for quote requests received on weekdays. A Friday evening inquiry receives a receipt explaining Monday coverage. The timer and dashboard use the same staffed-hours definition, preventing misleading weekend breaches.
failure: An automatic email that says someone will respond does not answer the buyer's question. Count acknowledgments separately from useful responses and check whether faster replies produce qualified conversations.
measure: Report median and slowest response ranges, unassigned inquiries, and qualified conversations by source. Investigate outliers instead of rewarding empty replies.

title: Sales Pipeline Aging Report Template and Review Rules
intro: A pipeline aging report shows how long opportunities remain in a stage and which buyer decision is holding them there. It helps a small sales team distinguish active evaluation from a deal that survives only in the forecast.
fields: Use a stable identifier and account name.
Preserve the date when stage evidence was first met.
Calculate from the entry date using one reporting convention.
Name the buyer action needed to progress.
Record the owner and dated follow-up.
Advance, hold with reason, nurture, or close with reason.
steps: Group opportunities by stage and deal type. A complex implementation and a repeat purchase should not share one arbitrary aging threshold.
Review older opportunities against documented buyer evidence. Ask what changed since the last review and who owns the next decision.
Remove unsupported close dates and record an honest disposition. Use the history to revise qualification and stage definitions.
example: Illustrative example: a proposal has been open for 45 days. The seller reports enthusiasm, but the buyer has not confirmed a budget owner or review date. The manager moves it out of the near-term forecast and schedules a qualification conversation. Age triggers investigation; it does not automatically prove the deal is lost.
failure: Resetting stage dates to make a report look healthier hides the bottleneck. Preserve meaningful history and record why an opportunity re-entered a stage.
measure: Track stage duration, repeated close-date slips, and conversion by opportunity cohort. Review closed losses as well as wins to avoid a biased cycle-time estimate.

title: Project Margin Review Template for Service Firms
intro: A project margin review compares the economics sold with the economics delivered. Use a consistent cost definition so an apparently successful project does not hide unrecorded labor, rework, or subcontractor expenses.
fields: Use a consistent project revenue figure and timing convention.
Record actual hours and an agreed internal cost rate.
Include subcontractors, materials, and project-specific purchases.
Separate correction effort from planned delivery.
Link approved additions and unpriced extra work.
Assign a cause and an owner for the next pricing or delivery change.
steps: Agree with finance on the meaning of project margin and which costs belong in it. Do not compare one project's gross margin with another project's fully allocated profit.
Review hours and purchases while the project is active. Waiting for final invoicing makes it harder to correct scope, staffing, or supplier choices.
Compare the estimate with actual delivery by work package. Feed recurring differences into future estimates and scope language.
example: Illustrative example: a $20,000 project has $9,000 in delivery labor and $3,000 in external costs. Under that defined direct-cost basis, contribution is $8,000, or 40%. An additional $2,000 of unrecorded rework would reduce it to 30%. Neither figure includes general overhead unless your chosen method allocates it.
failure: Treating an owner's unpaid delivery time as free can make a service look scalable when it relies on hidden labor. Record the time even if finance reports its cost separately.
measure: Compare quoted and actual hours, direct margin under the agreed definition, and unapproved scope effort. Investigate variance before imposing a blanket price increase.

title: Employee Cross-Training Matrix Template for Small Teams
intro: A cross-training matrix shows which essential tasks have qualified coverage when the usual person is absent. It distinguishes someone who has watched a task from someone who can perform and verify it independently.
fields: Choose a task whose interruption would affect delivery.
Use observed, supervised, independent, or able to train.
Link a completed practice run and reviewer feedback.
Record a review date and any access or certification requirements.
steps: List the tasks that stop when one person takes leave. Prioritize customer deadlines, cash collection, and operational access.
Provide the backup with a current procedure and appropriate access. Practice in a safe environment before assigning live responsibility.
Have the backup perform a complete cycle while the primary observes. Update the procedure when an undocumented judgment or exception appears.
example: Illustrative example: only the office manager can prepare the weekly scheduling file. A backup first observes, then produces a draft using a sample week. The manager checks constraints and corrections. Independent status is granted after a successful full cycle, rather than after a calendar invitation labeled training.
failure: A green spreadsheet cell does not prove readiness. Access can expire and rarely used skills can fade, so validate high-impact tasks before planned absences.
measure: Monitor critical tasks with no validated backup, practice failures, and interruptions during leave. Reassess coverage whenever roles or software change.

title: Owner Vacation Business Continuity Checklist
intro: An owner vacation continuity checklist turns a short absence into a controlled test of delegated operations. Prepare decision limits and emergency coverage before leaving so the team can act without guessing what requires a call.
fields: Name the person coordinating decisions during the absence.
Specify spending, refunds, commitments, and hiring limits.
List customer, payroll, vendor, and reporting dates.
Verify authorized backups can reach required systems.
Define the conditions requiring immediate escalation.
Schedule a discussion of exceptions and unclear ownership.
steps: Review the calendar and open commitments with your acting lead. Resolve predictable approvals in advance without hiding unresolved risks.
Run a one-day rehearsal while you remain available. Record interruptions and turn recurring questions into clear authority or procedure updates.
Use an agreed reporting rhythm during the absence. On return, review outcomes with the team and improve the system before the next longer absence.
example: Illustrative example: a contractor's owner takes five working days away. The project manager can reschedule crews and approve routine purchases within a stated limit, while a safety incident triggers the emergency procedure and a call. Customer updates continue through the office coordinator instead of waiting for the owner's return.
failure: Sharing personal passwords creates fragile coverage. Establish individually authorized access and recovery arrangements before the absence, using the controls appropriate to each system.
measure: Count avoidable interruptions, delayed decisions, missed commitments, and exceptions resolved independently within the agreed limits.

title: Weekly Operations Scorecard Template for Service Teams
intro: A weekly operations scorecard brings demand, delivery, quality, and capacity into one short review. Its purpose is to prompt an operating decision while there is still time to change the outcome.
fields: State the numerator, denominator, and reporting period.
Identify the system or report used.
Assign one person to validate the number.
Show the same weekly cutoff for each period.
Agree on the condition requiring discussion.
Record one response with an owner and due date.
steps: Choose a small set of measures connected to current delivery constraints. Include backlog, due work, rework, and available capacity before adding decorative charts.
Define every measure with an example. Two managers should calculate the same result from the same records.
Review exceptions first, assign actions, and close the loop next week. Remove metrics that repeatedly fail to inform a decision.
example: Illustrative example: a service team completes 18 of 20 jobs due this week, giving a 90% on-time completion rate under its agreed definition. A separate rework count shows three completed jobs needed correction. Reading both numbers prevents the team from improving speed by accepting poor quality.
failure: Changing denominators between weeks makes trends meaningless. Document whether rescheduled jobs remain in the original due-week cohort and apply that rule consistently.
measure: Track whether exceptions produce completed actions, how many numbers need manual correction, and whether the scorecard predicts customer-visible problems.

title: Automation Exception Handling Checklist for Small Businesses
intro: An automation exception checklist defines what happens when a workflow cannot safely finish. A useful automation needs a visible failure queue, a human owner, and a recovery path alongside its successful path.
fields: Define what starts the workflow and required data.
Check permissions, required fields, and acceptable formats.
Separate temporary failures from invalid input or business exceptions.
Define retry, correction, manual processing, or cancellation.
Record status, attempts, decisions, and final outcome.
steps: Map the manual process and identify actions that affect customers, money, or sensitive records. Decide which steps need human review.
Test missing fields, unavailable services, duplicates, and timeouts in a controlled environment. Verify that failures create a visible task rather than silently disappearing.
Define safe retry limits and prevent repeated execution from creating duplicate actions. Review the exception queue during the pilot before expanding volume.
example: Illustrative example: a signed agreement normally creates an onboarding project. A timeout occurs after the project is created but before confirmation returns. A retry checks the agreement's stable identifier before creating anything else, then routes an ambiguous result to a person. This prevents two teams from onboarding the same customer.
failure: An email alert alone is not an exception queue. Assign a state, owner, age, and closure record so unresolved failures remain visible after the notification is read.
measure: Report failed runs, duplicate actions, oldest unresolved exception, and recovery effort. Compare the total operating effort with the manual baseline.

title: AI Pilot Success Criteria Template for Business Workflows
intro: AI pilot success criteria define the business task, acceptable output, review effort, and conditions for stopping a trial. Write them before testing tools so impressive demonstrations do not substitute for reliable operating results.
fields: Specify the input, output, user, and workflow boundary.
Measure current completion time, error rate, and review effort.
Include ordinary, difficult, incomplete, and prohibited inputs.
Define quality requirements and human approval points.
Document approved information, access, retention, and vendor review.
Choose expand, revise, or stop using recorded evidence.
steps: Choose a repetitive task with observable outputs and a reversible failure mode. Avoid starting with autonomous high-impact customer or financial decisions.
Have a qualified reviewer score a fixed set of representative examples. Include verification time in the comparison with the existing workflow.
Pilot with a small group, log failures, and test whether a fallback works. Expand only after the team can explain both the benefit and the remaining limitations.
example: Illustrative example: an AI tool drafts internal meeting summaries. The pilot checks whether decisions, owners, and due dates match the transcript, and whether unsupported statements appear. If drafting saves ten minutes but verification takes fifteen, the pilot has not demonstrated a time saving even when the prose looks polished.
failure: A single accuracy percentage can conceal a serious failure type. Track fabricated commitments and missing actions separately from cosmetic wording issues.
measure: Compare total task time including review, correction rates by severity, user adoption, and fallback frequency. Record results as pilot observations rather than promises of future performance.

title: Vendor Performance Scorecard Template for Small Businesses
intro: A vendor performance scorecard turns repeated supplier frustrations into a documented operating conversation. Evaluate the commitments that affect customer delivery instead of ranking suppliers only by price.
fields: Define the product or service standard agreed with the supplier.
Record due dates, completeness, and accepted quantities.
Document defects and the basis for acceptance.
Track time to acknowledge and resolve exceptions.
Identify approved price changes and disputed charges.
Assign an owner, next review date, and fallback option.
steps: Choose a few important suppliers and gather actual orders or service records. Separate supplier-caused delays from changes your own team requested.
Review exceptions with supporting evidence and give the supplier an opportunity to correct misunderstandings.
Agree on a corrective action and review date. For critical dependencies, assess an alternative before a repeated failure becomes a customer emergency.
example: Illustrative example: a supplier delivers nine of ten orders on time but repeatedly omits one required component. Counting delivery dates alone gives a reassuring result. A complete-and-accepted measure exposes the issue, and the purchasing lead requests a packing verification step before the next order.
failure: Combining every measure into a weighted score can hide a critical defect behind a low price. Keep non-negotiable requirements visible as separate acceptance conditions.
measure: Monitor complete on-time deliveries, defect recurrence, and unresolved corrective actions. Review trends over a meaningful order sample rather than reacting to one isolated late shipment.

title: Multi-Location Manager Scorecard Template
intro: A multi-location manager scorecard compares operating performance using common definitions while preserving differences in site size and demand. It helps owners see which location needs support without turning every weekly call into anecdotal reporting.
fields: Use a comparable unit such as appointments, jobs, or orders.
Show staffed hours and relevant skill coverage.
Measure completed work and commitments missed.
Track corrections or complaints using a shared definition.
Document a site-specific issue affecting the numbers.
Record the decision, accountable manager, and review date.
steps: Agree on definitions across locations before comparing results. Normalize where appropriate, such as output per staffed hour, but retain raw totals for context.
Pilot the scorecard at two sites and ask managers to independently calculate the same sample period.
Discuss one operating constraint per site and share practices only after checking that the local conditions are comparable.
example: Illustrative example: one location completes 100 jobs with 200 staffed hours and another completes 70 with 100 hours. Raw volume favors the larger site, while jobs per hour favors the smaller one. Quality, job complexity, and customer waiting time are needed before concluding which operating method is better.
failure: A league table can encourage managers to move work between weeks or underreport corrections. Define cutoffs and review source records when unusual improvements appear.
measure: Track definition consistency, unresolved site constraints, and customer outcomes alongside volume. Verify improvements persist after staffing and demand change.

title: Post-Acquisition Employee Transition Checklist for Operators
intro: A post-acquisition employee transition checklist organizes the operational handover after a business changes ownership. Use it to clarify contacts, responsibilities, and immediate delivery continuity alongside the work handled by legal, finance, and HR advisers.
fields: Name the person employees can ask about operational issues.
Confirm who owns current customer and internal commitments.
List systems requiring authorized access updates.
Record what can be communicated, by whom, and when.
Identify tasks held by one person and arrange documented coverage.
Track unresolved questions with an owner and next update date.
steps: Map critical customer deadlines and the people who know how to meet them. Preserve delivery continuity while reviewing the inherited operating model.
Coordinate employee communications with the advisers responsible for transaction and employment matters. Avoid promising terms or changes that have not been approved.
Meet team leads, record operational uncertainties, and establish a short review cadence. Sequence improvements so the business can absorb them without losing essential knowledge.
example: Illustrative example: a newly acquired service company relies on one scheduler who knows customer access requirements from memory. The incoming operator pairs a backup with the scheduler, captures the next two weeks of requirements, and confirms escalation contacts before replacing the scheduling tool.
failure: Changing titles, systems, and reporting lines simultaneously can erase the context needed to diagnose problems. Maintain a decision log and explain the purpose and owner of each transition action.
measure: Monitor missed customer commitments, unresolved employee questions, critical tasks without backups, and access issues during the transition.

title: Project Closeout Checklist for Professional Services Firms
intro: A professional services project closeout checklist confirms that delivery, acceptance, billing, and knowledge transfer are complete. It prevents a project from remaining half-open after the team has mentally moved to its next assignment.
fields: List the agreed outputs and evidence of completion.
Record the acceptance method required by the agreement.
Assign unresolved issues, owners, and dates.
Reconcile approved changes, expenses, and invoice status.
Identify files, instructions, and support contacts handed over.
Capture estimate variance and changes for the next project.
steps: Review the signed scope and approved changes with the project owner. Separate incomplete contractual work from optional future recommendations.
Confirm acceptance and outstanding support responsibilities with the customer using the agreed process. Record any conditions rather than marking every item complete prematurely.
Reconcile billing and archive records with appropriate access. Hold a short delivery review while the details are still fresh.
example: Illustrative example: a consultant completes a workflow redesign but the client has not received the administrator instructions. The closeout checklist catches the missing transfer, assigns a handover session, and leaves that item open until completion. Final delivery status then reflects what the client can actually operate.
failure: Closing a project in the project management tool does not close its financial or customer obligations. Make each closeout status explicit and coordinate with the person responsible for invoicing.
measure: Track days from final delivery to acceptance, unbilled approved work, unresolved closeout items, and repeat support questions caused by missing handover information.
